title: Appeals Court Revives Missouri GOP Gerrymander After Supreme Court Dismisses It Twice
body:
A federal appeals panel on Monday reinstated a Republican‑drawn congressional map in Missouri, overturning a decision by the state’s Supreme Court that had sharply rebuked Secretary of State Jay Ashcroft’s redistricting plan. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the lower court’s order—issued after the Missouri Supreme Court found the map unconstitutional—was “procedurally improper,” effectively reviving a districting scheme that the state’s highest court had struck down twice.

The controversy began in 2021 when Missouri’s Republican‑controlled legislature adopted a new congressional map that packed Democratic‑leaning precincts into a single district while spreading Republican voters across the remaining three. Critics argued the design violated the state constitution’s guarantee of fair representation. After a series of lawsuits, the Missouri Supreme Court, in a 5‑2 decision, declared the map an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander and ordered the state to redraw the lines. The court’s opinion warned that the plan “dilutes the voting power of a substantial number of citizens” and set a precedent for future challenges to partisan redistricting.

State officials, led by Ashcroft, appealed the ruling to the federal courts, contending that the state Supreme Court had overstepped its authority by injecting a political judgment into a matter traditionally governed by federal law. The 8th Circuit agreed, holding that the Missouri Supreme Court’s order “exceeds the bounds of its jurisdiction” and that the lower federal district court should have stayed the decision pending appeal. By vacating the state court’s injunction, the appellate panel cleared the way for the original GOP‑crafted map to remain in place for the 2024 elections.

Legal scholars note that the case underscores a growing clash between state constitutions and federal oversight of redistricting. While the U.S. Supreme Court has repeatedly declined to hear partisan gerrymander claims, citing a lack of judicially manageable standards, several state courts have stepped in to fill the gap. Missouri’s Supreme Court, for example, invoked its own constitutional provisions to strike down the map, a move mirrored in recent decisions from Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin. The 8th Circuit’s reversal, however, signals that federal appellate courts may be reluctant to endorse state‑level partisan gerrymander bans when they conflict with the federal judiciary’s more restrained approach.

Political implications are immediate. With the map restored, Missouri’s congressional delegation is likely to retain a solid Republican majority, mirroring the party’s dominance in the state legislature and the governor’s office. Democrats argue that the decision disenfranchises roughly 300,000 voters in the state’s 1st and 2nd districts, whose communities of interest have been fragmented across multiple districts. Republican leaders, meanwhile, hail the ruling as a vindication of “the will of the people” and warn that further judicial interference would undermine electoral stability.

The battle is far from over. Ashcroft’s office has indicated it will seek a stay from the U.S. Supreme Court, while Democratic plaintiffs are preparing a new challenge that could argue the map violates the Voting Rights Act’s protections against racial vote dilution. Moreover, the case may prompt other states with similar partisan maps to test the limits of state constitutional provisions versus federal judicial restraint. As the 2024 election cycle accelerates, courts at every level will likely become arenas for the next front line in the national debate over how political power is drawn and distributed.
